title: SQL
subtitle: The language of relational databases, from a first SELECT to joins, recursive queries, window functions, query plans, transactions and a schema of your own design.
description: SQL is the language for defining, changing and asking questions of data held in relational databases. It grew out of IBM research in the early 1970s (the first version, called SEQUEL, was described in 1974), became an ANSI and ISO standard in the 1980s, and is still revised every few years. Nearly every application that keeps records talks to a database in SQL: websites and phone apps, banks and hospitals, scientific archives, and the analytics warehouses where companies study their own data. Its signature idea is that you describe *what* result you want and let the database work out *how* to compute it.

This course is for people who can already program a little: if you know what a variable, a loop and a function are (the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience), you are ready. Lumenary CS has a general [Databases](/en/cs/databases/) lesson on why databases exist and how they work inside; this course goes much deeper into the language itself. It teaches standard SQL and runs every example on SQLite, and it points out where PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite differ, so that what you learn carries over to whichever database you meet at work.

To follow along, install the `sqlite3` command-line shell from [sqlite.org/download.html](https://www.sqlite.org/download.html) (it is already present on most macOS and Linux systems), or try queries in the official [SQLite Fiddle](https://sqlite.org/fiddle/), which runs SQLite in your browser with nothing to install. For a server database, install PostgreSQL from [postgresql.org/download](https://www.postgresql.org/download/). Every program marked as checked was run by Lumenary's test suite with the SQLite 3.37 shell, and the output shown is the output it printed. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.summary: Where SQL came from and the relational model behind it, then tables, types and constraints, changing data safely, and filtering and sorting rows, including the three-valued logic that NULL brings.

levels.title: Practice
levels.summary: The everyday power tools: aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING, joins of every kind, subqueries, common table expressions (recursive ones too) and views, and window functions for rankings, running totals and comparisons between rows.

levels.title: Professional
levels.summary: How databases make queries fast and keep data correct under concurrency, then normalisation, JSON columns and a complete schema designed and queried from scratch.
